pages.title: Notes
pages.content: Dispatches from our counter, prep room and cellar: how the ice is cut, and what we pour after dark.

posts.title: Tuesday Is Ice Day
posts.excerpt: Every Tuesday morning, bar back Theo Lambrecht breaks down a twenty-five-kilogram block of clear ice into five-centimeter cubes for the week ahead.
posts.content:
Every Tuesday at ten in the morning, while the bar is closed and our basement on Maanstraat is silent, a heavy insulated crate arrives at the basement door. Inside rests a single twenty-five-kilogram block of directional-frozen ice, perfectly clear from edge to edge without a cloud or fissure. For the next three hours, before the rest of Ghent gathers for lunch, our prep bench belongs to a hand saw, a serrated knife, and a pair of heavy rubber gloves. Preparing ice is neither glamorous nor fast, but it is the physical foundation of every stirred drink we pour between Wednesday and Sunday.

Most people think of ice as an afterthought, something that simply cools a liquid until it melts. In reality, ice is the most critical ingredient in a stirred cocktail. When water freezes slowly from the top down, air bubbles and minerals are pushed to the bottom and discarded, leaving a solid block of pure, crystalline density. Because this dense ice contains no pockets of trapped air, it melts at a predictable, controlled rate. When we place a five-centimeter cube into a mixing glass with gin and vermouth, it drops the temperature rapidly while releasing only the exact volume of water necessary to open the spirit's aromatic compounds.

Breaking down a twenty-five-kilogram block requires steady rhythm rather than brute force. I begin by scoring lines across the surface with a steel ruler and a serrated blade, marking out precise grids across the clear ice. Once a clean groove is established, a gentle tap on the spine of the knife cleaves the block into thick slabs. From those slabs, I cut uniform five-centimeter cubes, trimming irregular corners and discarding chips into the prep sink. By one in the afternoon, sixty individual cubes sit stacked inside our freezer trays, completely dry and tempered so they will not crack when liquid meets them at the counter.

This Tuesday routine connects directly to the five steps of our cocktail build. When Margit, Lucía, or Kofi stands behind the walnut counter during evening service, there is no guessing about dilution. Step 01 is always one of these hand-cut cubes. In step 02, the spirits are measured strictly by jigger. Step 03 is forty turns with the barspoon—about thirty seconds of smooth rotation where the cube glides against the glass wall without chipping. Step 04 strains the chilled liquid into a coupe pulled straight from our −18 °C freezer, and step 05 expresses citrus oils before discarding the peel.

When guests take their seats at 19:00 on Wednesday evening, the counter is polished, the brass lamps are lit, and the afternoon prep work has vanished from sight. Hana opens the reservation book, Samir slices dark rye in the back, and the first mixing glasses are set out on the walnut wood. When you look down into your glass and see a single clear cube resting silently beneath the surface, that clarity began here on Tuesday morning. In a basement with twelve seats and a short list, doing one thing thoroughly by hand is what gives the room its quiet confidence.

posts.title: Why Twelve Seats
posts.excerpt: Twelve seats is the number at which Hana can still greet every guest by name and Samir can still see every glass.
posts.content:
Twelve seats is the number at which Hana can still greet every guest by name and Samir can still see every glass. We tried a longer counter in the planning stage and it felt like a different bar: the bartender spent the evening walking instead of stirring. So the arc stays at twelve, with three seatings on Wednesday to Sunday evenings at 19:00, 21:00 and 23:00.

A small room also keeps the list short. Every drink on it has to be built within a minute or two, by hand, in front of the person who ordered it. If you would like one of the twelve, bookings open fourteen days ahead at 12:00.

posts.title: The Counter Board
posts.excerpt: Samir slices dark rye each afternoon for the €12 Counter Board that goes with the first round.
posts.content:
Each afternoon before service, Samir slices dark rye by hand and lays it out beside cultured butter, pickled shallots and a small wedge of aged cheese. It is the €12 Counter Board, and it is meant to go with the first round rather than replace dinner.

We keep it plain on purpose. The kitchen is a single bench at the back of the room, and the board is what that bench does best. Last orders are at 00:30, and the board is served until then.
